title: Distributed Computing Through Combinatorial Topology
byline: Maurice Herlihy, Dmitry Kozlov and Sergio Rajsbaum · Morgan Kaufmann, 2013
note: Chapter notes, problems and bibliography are not broken out; many chapters have no section entries in the PDF outline, so they appear as single leaves. Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: A textbook showing that what fault-tolerant distributed systems can compute is a question about topology. Processes’ possible views form simplicial complexes, protocols are maps between complexes, and a task is solvable exactly when a suitable simplicial map exists. Starting from two-process systems, the book develops the combinatorial topology it needs (complexes, subdivisions, connectivity), characterizes colorless tasks in wait-free, t-resilient, message-passing and Byzantine models, and introduces simulations such as BG. The second half treats general (colored) tasks: manifold protocols, connectivity arguments for consensus and k-set agreement impossibility, the asynchronous computability theorem, renaming and orientation, reductions between shared-memory models, loop agreement classified by the fundamental group, and the immediate snapshot subdivision.
